beats.text: Nobody typed it on a phone.
beats.note: It was sent from a computer. On 3 December 1992 an engineer at a desktop pushed two words onto the Vodafone network: Merry Christmas.

beats.name: Neil Papworth
beats.role: A 22-year-old test engineer, sending it to Vodafone director Richard Jarvis at the company Christmas party. His team had spent a year building the Short Message Service, meant not for chatting, but as a kind of pager.

beats.text: He had no way to text back.
beats.note: Phones then could receive a message but not compose one. The reply came as a phone call, from the party, to say it had worked.

beats.lead: And it stayed clumsy for years
beats.text: You could not text someone on a rival network until 1999.
beats.note: Handsets only gained a way to send texts in 1993, and every message was capped at 160 characters by the network's bandwidth: the pinch that bred txt spk like LOL.

beats.text: The text that started it all got no text in reply: the phone could not send one.

beats.line: The first text said 'Merry Christmas', computer to a phone that could not answer.
